text.en: Ira, daughter of an ironsmith, watches a grand procession of soldiers, horses and elephants cross the drawbridge. She tells visitors that it takes almost two months on horseback to reach the borders of the land. That is bigger than a kingdom, they say. What do we call it? An empire. In this chapter we see how empires arose, from Magadha to the Mauryas.

An empire is a very large territory that includes many smaller kingdoms under one ruler, the emperor. Regional kings or chiefs often continued to govern their areas in return for tribute, a payment given as a sign of loyalty, and respect. Empires rose, expanded, lasted for a while, declined and disappeared. When many smaller kingdoms warred, the one with stronger military power and surplus resources became the overlord. Building an empire needs economic power, control over people to work and fight, and access to resources.
Textiles, spices, farm produce, gems, handicrafts and animals were traded, as shown by literature and excavations. Traders formed guilds, associations of merchants or craftspeople that set rules and shared risks. They were remarkable institutions because they helped trade across regions and even lent money. The ancient village, with committees and councils, was another unit of organisation.
Of the sixteen mahajanapadas, Magadha grew strongest. It lay in the Ganga plains, which had fertile land, forests for timber and elephants for the army, and also iron-rich areas. Under the Nanda dynasty, Magadha grew rich and powerful, but the last Nanda king, Dhana Nanda, became very unpopular.
Alexander of Macedon came to the northwest of India about 326 BCE. According to Greek accounts he defeated, among others, the Pauravas led by their king Porus, but his tired soldiers refused to go further and he turned back. After he left, Greek governors called satraps were left behind, and back in Persia Alexander faced rebellions.
Chandragupta Maurya, guided by his teacher Kautilya (also known as Chanakya), overthrew the Nandas, defeated the Greek satraps in the northwest and built an empire that stretched from the northern plains to the Deccan plateau. Kautilya is credited with the Arthashastra, a text on governance, taxes, spies, the army and trade. Its idea of a state is a useful comparison with a modern nation. The Mauryas had a capital at Pataliputra with palaces, public buildings and well-planned streets, and a strong army and officers. Granaries were built to store grain as a precaution against famine, showing care for food security.
Ashoka, grandson of Chandragupta, ruled about 268 to 232 BCE. After the terrible Kalinga war, in which many people died, he gave up war and followed dharma, which means right conduct, compassion and respect for all sects. He told his own story in edicts, writings carved on rocks and pillars, mostly in Prakrit, the popular language, in the Brahmi script. They speak of his rest houses, wells and shade trees on the main roads and his officers' duty to care for the people. He wished to project the image of a benevolent ruler who encouraged his subjects to follow dharma. The Sanchi stupa, originally of brick and later enlarged in stone, and the lion capital of Ashoka are fine examples of Mauryan art.
The larger an empire becomes, the harder it is to hold together. Far-off territories are often the first to break away. After Ashoka the Mauryan empire gradually weakened and ended. Many other empires in world history rose and fell: the Persian, Roman, Ottoman, British and others. Empires are fragile, but their art, ideas and roads often remain.

problem.en: Why did Magadha become more powerful than other mahajanapadas?

text.en: Its location in the Ganga plains gave fertile farms.
Forests gave timber and elephants.
Iron-rich areas nearby gave better tools and weapons.

prompt.en: Describe Ashoka's dharma and how he spread it.

requiredIdeas.en: Right conduct, compassion, respect for all beliefs.
Rock and pillar edicts in Prakrit.
Wells, rest houses and shade trees.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking dharma meant one religion only.

points.en: An empire joins many kingdoms under one emperor.
Magadha, then the Nandas, then the Mauryas built the first large Indian empire.
Chandragupta and Kautilya built it; Ashoka followed dharma after Kalinga.
Empires are hard to hold together and eventually decline.
